summary: This document is a deep technical analysis by the Georgia Longevity Alliance (ARGUS project) addressing how to determine, using label-free light microscopy only, which daughter cell receives the older vs. newer centriole after mitosis. It reviews the published literature, identifies a weak morphological correlate (daughter size/spindle asymmetry from Thomas & Meraldi 2024), and proposes an empirical calibration strategy (Option E) as the only honest path to label-free centriole-age assignment. The honest conclusion is that unambiguous label-free determination is not currently possible, and marker-anchored methods remain the baseline.

content_blocks.title: Document Header and Context
content_blocks.content: Title: ARGUS — How to Determine, by Morphology Visible in Light Microscopy (No Staining), Which Daughter Will Receive the Older and Which the Newer Centriole after Mitosis. Author: Jaba Tqemaladze (Georgia Longevity Alliance). Date: 2026-10-21. Status: deep analysis of the question; single cell; first fibroblasts, then immortalized fibroblasts. Every claim carries a source (PMID/DOI). Companion documents: ARGUS_Protocol_v0.2, ARGUS_TRD_v0.9b, ARGUS_Literature_Analysis_EN.md. This is part of the ARGUS project, which appears to be a single-cell longevity/aging research program focused on centriole age asymmetry in cell division.

content_blocks.title: Section 1: Framing and Biology of Centriole Inheritance
content_blocks.content:
The core question is: using one cell, light microscopy only, no fluorescent staining — by which visible features (geometry, dimensions, shape, dynamics) can one determine, after mitosis, which daughter cell receives the oldest centriole and which the newest?

Biology: In G2 the cell has 4 centrioles: two 'mature' (M — inherited from the mother, age N generations; D — formed last cycle, now mature, age 1) and two new procentrioles (age 0). Two centrosomes: {M + new procentriole} and {D + new procentriole}. At mitosis each daughter receives one centrosome = one mature (mother) centriole + one new procentriole.

Key consequence: after mitosis BOTH daughters contain a newest (just-formed) centriole. The real asymmetry is in the mature centriole: one daughter receives the oldest M (founder lineage), the other the younger mature D (age 1). The task is therefore: determine which daughter receives the older mature (M) and which the younger mature (D).

content_blocks.title: Section 2: What Light Microscopy Can and Cannot See Without Staining
content_blocks.content:
Feature | Visible in LM without staining | Comment
Centriole as object (~200–250 nm) | NO | at/beyond diffraction limit (~250 nm at NA≈1.2); invisible without contrast
Mother-centriole appendages | NO | ~100 nm, EM only
PTM differences (age) | NO | molecular; invisible without staining
Pericentriolar-material differences | NO | beyond resolution without contrast
Daughter cell size/volume | YES (phase/DIC) | direct measurable feature
Spindle geometry, metaphase-plate position, asters | YES (DIC/phase/polarized) | spindle of ordered microtubules gives contrast; asters visible in polarization
Dry mass of the cell | YES (QPI — quantitative phase) | label-free, measurable
Dynamics (anaphase timing, aster movement) | YES (time-lapse DIC/phase) | kinetic feature

content_blocks.title: Section 3: Published Literature — Known Light-Microscopy Correlates of Centriole Age
content_blocks.content:
The only published light-microscopy correlate of centriole age in division is a mild spindle/daughter-size asymmetry:

- Thomas & Meraldi 2024 (J Cell Biol; PMID 39012627, DOI 10.1083/jcb.202311153): in human epithelial and fibroblastic lines, centriole age 'breaks spindle symmetry even in symmetric divisions' → unequal daughter sizes. Mechanism: the old centriole carries more Odf2/cenexin-bound Plk1 → higher microtubule nucleation (pericentrin, γ-tubulin, TPX2, ch-TOG) → the half-spindle on the old-centriole side is longer. Direct morphological consequence: without staining, by daughter size (and/or spindle asymmetry), one can probabilistically indicate where the older centriole is — but the effect is WEAK (not deterministic).

What does NOT exist in the literature:
- No method that unambiguously assigns the older centriole to one of two daughters in fibroblasts by geometry/size in light microscopy.
- No data for immortalized fibroblasts (BJ-hTERT/MRC5-hTERT) on centriole-age asymmetry at all — identified as a gap.
- No documented geometric rule ('older always to adhesion / to the right') for cultured fibroblasts (unlike Drosophila niche, where position is rigid; Yamashita 2007, PMID 17255513).

content_blocks.title: Section 4: Method Options — Label-Free Morphology Only
content_blocks.content:
Option A — Daughter size/volume (phase/DIC) [published]: Measure daughter areas/volumes at cytokinesis. The larger daughter is more likely to carry the older centriole. Pros: simple, cheap, live, no excitation light. Cons: weak effect (Thomas & Meraldi 2024) → in a single cell this is only a probability P ≈ 0.5+δ, δ small; insufficient for rigorous assignment. Fibroblasts: included in Thomas & Meraldi (weak effect present). Immortalized — no data.

Option B — Spindle/aster geometry (DIC/phase, polarized light) [mechanism published]: The half-spindle on the old-centriole side is longer; the aster on the old side is larger/brighter in polarization. Metrics: metaphase-plate offset from center; half-spindle length difference; aster intensity in polarized light; astral-MT asymmetry. Pros: directly reflects the mechanism (nucleation), label-free. Cons: requires polarization/quality optics and kinetic imaging; the 'side → daughter' + 'side → older' link remains probabilistic.

Option C — Quantitative phase / dry mass (QPI) [label-free, mature technique]: Phase/holographic microscopy gives dry mass of daughters; mass asymmetry is more quantitative than area. Pros: label-free, more accurate than A; suitable for long runs (not phototoxic). Cons: separate optics; link to centriole age remains weak (via size, as in A).

Option D — Division kinetics (time-lapse DIC/phase) [not proven for age]: Differences in anaphase-onset time, separation speed, cytokinesis symmetry between sides. Possibly correlates with nucleation asymmetry (B), but no direct data for centriole age — experimental hypothesis.

Option E — Empirical calibration of a morphological predictor (recommended) [plan, not literature]: Run a calibration phase on the same lines/conditions WITH fluorescent markers (Cep164 + age marker, pedigree) to obtain ground truth (which daughter got the older centriole). In parallel record a battery of label-free features: daughter size/volume, spindle asymmetry, plate offset, aster asymmetry in polarization, dry mass (QPI), kinetics. Train a classifier 'older goes to daughter A or B' on ground truth; report accuracy (e.g., % correct assignments per division). If accuracy ≥ 95%: assign OLD/NEW by morphology in working run. If below threshold: markers remain mandatory. Pros: the only honest path to 'label-free' in ARGUS; turns a weak effect into a verified metric; directly serves minimal phototoxicity. Cons: requires a marker calibration phase; accuracy depends on lines and effect size.

Option F — Pedigree bootstrap [NOT NEEDED in this experiment]: In the founder cell, without any anchor, 'which of two centrioles is older' cannot be determined by morphology alone. Not required here because the anchor exists — the founder's first division, where mother (mature, Cep164+) and newly formed (Cep164−) are distinguishable.

content_blocks.title: Section 5: Cell Line Specifics — Fibroblasts and Immortalized Fibroblasts
content_blocks.content:
Normal fibroblasts: the only known effect is the mild spindle/daughter-size asymmetry (Thomas & Meraldi 2024, included fibroblastic lines). No geometric inheritance rule documented.

Immortalized fibroblasts (BJ-hTERT/MRC5-hTERT): NO DATA AT ALL — neither on centriole-age asymmetry nor on a morphological correlate. This is an identified gap to be closed by pre-test V2/V3 (division behaviour, morphology) in the calibration phase with markers (Option E). This represents a key experimental gap in the ARGUS project.

content_blocks.title: Section 6: Honest Conclusions and Recommended Strategy
content_blocks.content:
1. By morphology alone, without staining, an unambiguous determination of which daughter receives the older centriole is NOT possible today: the only published correlate (size/spindle, Thomas & Meraldi 2024) is weak and probabilistic, and there are no data for immortalized fibroblasts.

2. The practical path compatible with 'no staining in the working run' is empirical calibration (Option E): a short marker phase gives ground truth; a label-free morphological classifier (daughter size + spindle + QPI + polarization + kinetics) is trained on it; if accuracy is high — work without fluorescent light (minimal phototoxicity). If label-free does not work (accuracy below threshold) — the same marker-anchored method (Cep164 + age marker + continuous pedigree) is applied at every division.

3. Logical boundary resolved: the first assignment in the founder cell does not require bootstrap — the first division anchors OLD/NEW (Cep164+ vs Cep164−). Thereafter label-free, calibrated morphology can be used if Option E succeeds.

4. For rigorous Q2/Q3 (protocol v0.2) the OLD/NEW assignment is marker-anchored (Cep164 + age marker + pedigree); label-free morphology serves as a calibrated secondary channel — and as a way to reduce the light load if calibration allows.

key_findings: The only published light-microscopy correlate of centriole age in division is a mild spindle/daughter-size asymmetry (Thomas & Meraldi 2024, PMID 39012627): the old centriole carries more Odf2/cenexin-bound Plk1 → higher MT nucleation → longer half-spindle on the old-centriole side → unequal daughter sizes.
The effect is WEAK and probabilistic (P ≈ 0.5+δ, δ small); unambiguous label-free assignment of centriole age to a specific daughter cell is NOT currently possible.
No data exist for immortalized fibroblasts (BJ-hTERT/MRC5-hTERT) on centriole-age asymmetry or morphological correlates — identified as a critical experimental gap.
No geometric inheritance rule ('older always to adhesion / to the right') has been documented for cultured fibroblasts.

Proposed solution (Option E): empirical calibration phase using fluorescent markers (Cep164 + age marker + pedigree) to generate ground truth, then train a label-free morphological classifier; if accuracy ≥ 95%, working runs can proceed without fluorescent staining.
Marker-anchored method (Cep164 + age marker + continuous pedigree) remains the baseline for rigorous OLD/NEW centriole assignment in Q2/Q3 (protocol v0.2).
The first division of the founder cell anchors OLD/NEW assignment: Cep164+ daughter → OLD branch; Cep164− daughter → NEW branch. No bootstrap required.
Cell lines of interest: normal fibroblasts (weak effect documented) and immortalized fibroblasts BJ-hTERT/MRC5-hTERT (no data — gap to be closed by pre-test V2/V3).
Key reference: Yamashita 2007 (PMID 17255513) — Drosophila niche shows rigid positional inheritance rule, but no equivalent documented for cultured fibroblasts.
Project is at an early conceptual/planning stage (TRL 1–2): no experiments have been completed; the document is a literature review and experimental design analysis.
